text: Can we predict part geometry during printing?

name: TextBox 5
text:
▪  Directed Energy Deposition (DED) builds metal parts track by track — but final geometry varies along every track.
▪  In-situ sensors watch the melt pool in real time; post-process metrology reveals what was actually built — hours later.
▪  The challenge: connect what the camera sees during printing to the local geometric variation measured after printing.
▪  If we can do this, we unlock real-time quality prediction and closed-loop control for metal additive manufacturing.

name: TextBox 5
text:
▪  Thermal warping: the metal substrate bows during printing, so a perfectly rigid 2D plane fit cannot capture all deformation.
▪  Deep gouges in the substrate produce some negative ground-truth heights (down to −40 µm) after leveling.
▪  Model uncertainty grows in regions of extreme substrate deformation — exactly where the plane assumption weakens.
▪  R² = 0.41 reflects genuine stochasticity in DED, not just model error — a meaningful signal in a noisy physical process.
